The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.
This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and "pee on your brain."
The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Mr. Huang's management style.

Mr. Huang's behavior rubbed off on other senior leaders at the company, including his daughter, Madison. On one call last year with Nvidia's marketing team, Ms.
Huang repeatedly berated a vice president, who then left the call, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by The Times.
"I'm having an anxiety attack," the vice president said. "I'm going to drop off. I'm sorry."
Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment.

Employing the CEO's relatives was already a governance risk. If the outside agitation continues to reinstate Jensen Huang, there are three key lambs that Nvidia can slaughter, and all of them are his relatives. I suppose the thing I find most astonishing is that Huang doesn't see the writing on the wall; he has posted that if "the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." The post was met with, among other things, Altman posting a green heart in response.
